summary.text: The Achaemenid Empire was an ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC and based on the Iranian plateau.
At its peak it covered roughly 5.5 million square kilometres, the largest empire of its time, stretching from the Balkans in the west to the Indus Valley in the east.
Alexander the Great conquered it entirely in 330 BC, and most of its lands then came under the Seleucid Empire and the Ptolemaic Kingdom.

paragraphs.heading: The Kingdom
paragraphs.text: The Achaemenid Empire was an ancient Iranian empire, founded in 550 BC by Cyrus the Great of the Achaemenid dynasty. Its own Old Persian name, Xšāça, simply meant The Kingdom. At its height it covered roughly 5.5 million square kilometres, more than any other empire of its day. From its base on the Iranian plateau it spread westward to the Balkans and Cyrenaica and eastward to the Indus Valley, taking in Anatolia, Mesopotamia, the Levant and large parts of Central Asia.

paragraphs.heading: Who the Persians were
paragraphs.text: The empire is named after Achaemenes, credited as founder of the dynasty, a minor ruler of Anshan in southwestern Iran in the seventh century and a vassal of Assyria. The Persians who built it were an Iranic people who came to what is now Iran around 1000 BC and lived at first as nomadic herders on the western Iranian plateau. They settled lands including the Zagros Mountains and Persis alongside the native Elamites. The word Persia is how Greek and Latin pronounced the native name for the land of the people from Persis.

paragraphs.heading: Cyrus takes Media
paragraphs.text: Its rulers began as kings of Anshan, an Elamite city. The Cyrus Cylinder, the oldest surviving family tree of the dynasty, lists the kings of Anshan down to Cyrus II, known as Cyrus the Great. In 553 BC Cyrus rose up against the Median Empire; three years later, in 550, he beat the Medes, captured their king Astyages and seized their capital, Ecbatana. He then claimed to be Astyages' heir and took over his whole empire, along with its old quarrels with Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

paragraphs.heading: Lydia and Babylon
paragraphs.text: Croesus, king of Lydia, pushed into former Median land in Asia Minor, but Cyrus struck back, captured Sardis and ended the Lydian kingdom in 546 BC; bringing Lydia fully under control took about four years. In October 539 BC Cyrus beat the Babylonians in battle at Opis and then captured Babylon itself, taking its king Nabonidus prisoner. He is credited with freeing the Jews from captivity in Babylon, letting them go back to Judah and rebuild Jerusalem and its Second Temple.

paragraphs.heading: Growth and limits
paragraphs.text: By defeating Media, Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, Cyrus set up a new imperial power in the ancient Near East. When he died in 530 BC, his eldest son Cambyses II succeeded him. The empire went on growing quickly, but it was turned back from Scythia in 513 BC and from Greece twice, in 492 to 490 and in 480 to 479 BC.

paragraphs.heading: Conquered by Alexander
paragraphs.text: In 330 BC, in the middle of a Macedonian campaign that had begun in 336, Alexander the Great conquered the whole Achaemenid Empire and added it to his own. After his death in 323 BC, which opened the Hellenistic period, most of its lands passed to the Seleucid Empire and the Ptolemaic Kingdom. Almost a century later, Iranian elites took power back from the Seleucids and founded the Parthian Empire, which lasted nearly 500 years before the Sasanian Empire followed it.
